'''Transaction Logic''' is an extension of [[predicate logic]] that accounts in a clean and declarative way for the phenomenon of state changes in [[logic program]]s and [[database]]s. This extension adds connectives specifically designed for combining simple actions into complex transactions and for providing control over their execution. The logic has a natural [[model theory]] and a sound and complete [[proof theory]]. Transaction Logic has a [[Horn clause]] subset, which has a procedural as well as a declarative semantics. The important features of the logic include hypothetical and committed updates, dynamic constraints on transaction execution, non-determinism, and bulk updates.  In this way, Transaction Logic is able to declaratively capture a number of non-logical phenomena, including [[procedural knowledge]] in [[artificial intelligence]], [[active database]]s, and methods with side effects in [[object database]]s.

Transaction Logic was originally proposed in 1993 by [http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~bonner/ Anthony Bonner] and [http://www.cs.stonybrook.edu/~kifer/ Michael Kifer]<ref name="tr-iclp1993">A.J. Bonner and M. Kifer (1993), ''Transaction Logic Programming'', International Conference on Logic Programming (ICLP), 1993.</ref> and later described in more detail in ''An Overview of Transaction Logic''<ref>A.J. Bonner and M. Kifer (1994), ''An Overview of Transaction Logic'', Theoretical Computer Science, 133:2, 1994.</ref> and ''Logic Programming for Database Transactions''.<ref>A.J. Bonner and M. Kifer (1998), [http://www.cs.sunysb.edu/~kifer/TechReports/tr-chomicki.pdf ''Logic Programming for Database Transactions''] in Logics for Databases and Information Systems, J. Chomicki and G. Saake (eds.), Kluwer Academic Publ., 1998.</ref> The most comprehensive description appears in Bonner & Kifer's technical report from 1995.<ref>A.J. Bonner and M. Kifer (1995), [http://www.cs.sunysb.edu/~kifer/TechReports/transaction-logic.pdf ''Transaction Logic Programming (or A Logic of Declarative and Procedural Knowledge)'']. Technical Report CSRI-323, November 1995, Computer Science Research Institute, University of Toronto.</ref>

In later years, Transaction Logic was extended in various ways, including [[concurrency (computer science)|concurrency]],<ref name="concurrentTR">A.J. Bonner and M. Kifer (1996), [http://www.cs.sunysb.edu/~kifer/TechReports/concurrent-trans-logic.pdf ''Concurrency and communication in Transaction Logic''], Joint Intl. Conference and Symposium on Logic Programming, Bonn, Germany, September 1996</ref> [[defeasible reasoning]],<ref>P. Fodor and M. Kifer (2011), [http://drops.dagstuhl.de/opus/volltexte/2011/3159/ ''Transaction Logic with Defaults and Argumentation Theories'']. In Technical communications of the 27th International Conference on Logic Programming (ICLP), July 2011.</ref> partially defined actions,<ref>M. Rezk and M. Kifer (2012), [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs13740-012-0007-8 ''Transaction Logic with Partially Defined Actions'']. Journal on Data Semantics, August 2012, vol. 1, no. 2, Springer.</ref> and other features.<ref>H. Davulcu, M. Kifer and I.V. Ramakrishnan (2004), [http://www.www2004.org/proceedings/docs/2p144.pdf CTR-S: A Logic for Specifying Contracts in Semantic Web Services]. Proceedings of the 13-th World Wide Web Conference (WWW2004), May 2004.</ref><ref>P. Fodor and M. Kifer (2010), [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.184.6968 ''Tabling for Transaction Logic'']. In Proceedings of the 12th international ACM SIGPLAN symposium on Principles and practice of declarative programming (PPDP), July 2010.</ref>

In 2013, the original paper on Transaction Logic has [https://www.cs.stonybrook.edu/about-us/News/ALP-Presents-Prof-Kifer-20-year-Test-Time-Award won] the [https://www.cs.nmsu.edu/ALP/the-association-for-logic-programming/alp-awards/ 20-year Test of Time Award] of the [[Association for Logic Programming]] as the most influential paper from the proceedings of [http://www.informatik.uni-trier.de/~ley/db/conf/iclp/iclp93.html ICLP 1993 conference] in the preceding 20 years.

== Examples ==

=== Graph coloring ===
Here {{mono|tinsert}} denotes the elementary update operation of ''transactional insert''. The connective {{mono|⊗}} is called ''serial conjunction''.
<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
colorNode <-  // color one node correctly
    node(N) ⊗ ¬ colored(N,_) ⊗ color(C)
    ⊗ ¬(adjacent(N,N2) ∧ colored(N2,C))
    ⊗ tinsert(colored(N,C)).
colorGraph <- ¬uncoloredNodesLeft.
colorGraph <- colorNode ⊗ colorGraph.
</syntaxhighlight>

=== Pyramid stacking ===
The elementary update {{mono|tdelete}} represents the ''transactional delete'' operation.
<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
stack(N,X) <- N>0 ⊗ move(Y,X) ⊗ stack(N-1,Y).
stack(0,X).
move(X,Y) <- pickup(X) ⊗ putdown(X,Y).
pickup(X) <- clear(X) ⊗ on(X,Y) ⊗
             ⊗ tdelete(on(X,Y)) ⊗ tinsert(clear(Y)).
putdown(X,Y) <-  wider(Y,X) ⊗ clear(Y) 
                 ⊗ tinsert(on(X,Y)) ⊗ tdelete(clear(Y)).
</syntaxhighlight>

=== Hypothetical execution ===
Here {{mono|&lt;&gt;}} is the [[modal operator]] of possibility: If both {{mono|action1}} and {{mono|action2}} are possible, execute {{mono|action1}}. Otherwise, if only {{mono|action2}} is possible, then execute it.
<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
execute <- <>action1 ⊗ <>action2 ⊗ action1.
execute <- ¬<>action1 ⊗ <>action2 ⊗ action2.
</syntaxhighlight>

=== Dining philosophers ===
Here {{mono|1={{!}} }} is the [[logical connective]] of parallel conjunction of Concurrent Transaction Logic.<ref name="concurrentTR"/>
<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
diningPhilosophers <- phil(1) | phil(2) | phil(3) | phil(4).
</syntaxhighlight>

== Implementations ==
A number of implementations of Transaction Logic exist:
* The original implementation.<ref>{{cite web |last= Hung |first= Samuel |date= 1996 |title= Transaction Logic Prototype |publisher= University of Toronto, Department of Computer Science |url= http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~bonner/transaction-logic.html |access-date= 2021-05-10}}</ref>
* An implementation of Concurrent Transaction Logic.<ref>{{cite web |last= Sleghel |first= Amalia F. |date= 2000 |title= Concurrent Transaction Logic Prototype |publisher= University of Toronto, Department of Computer Science |url= http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~bonner/ctr/index.html |access-date= 2021-05-10}}</ref>
* Transaction Logic enhanced with [[tabling]]. An implementation of Transaction Logic has also been incorporated as part of the [[Flora-2]] knowledge representation and reasoning system.<ref>{{cite web |title= Knowledge Representation & Reasoning with Flora-2 |publisher= Sourceforge.net |url= http://flora.sourceforge.net |access-date= 2021-05-10}}</ref>

All these implementations are [[open source]].
